b: I have been working for a small nonprofit (less than 12 people) for a year. In September I was told that I was going to be laid off on December 1 due to a new strategic direction and funding cuts that would need to go towards professional fundraising consultants.

I’m not upset that I am getting laid off — I was job searching anyway — since my current org is a disaster (I mean people not showing up, not answering emails/delaying projects, having anxiety attacks and taking off multiple days in a row, verbal aggression, extreme toxicity, managers using manipulative strategies to get what they want). The list goes on and on.

This is my fifth layoff since 2021 and that in itself is hitting me hard. But I know the sites and I am not afraid of networking and using connections to land a role and I have a plan. What I am struggling are a few things:
1. Laziness is rewarded. There are a couple folks who don’t do their work and have caused significant delays in projects and deadlines but they kept their jobs.
2. Why me? I have been an asset to the team, often taking on others’ work (or given it) because I had the time and they knew I could be counted on.
3. Since I have two months, I am really having hard time staying focused and wanting to do work or even being engaged in conversation with people.

4. I applied to a role using a connection, and she wrote me an amazing letter of recommendation. My boyfriend and best friend both assured me I would at least get a screening, but I got rejected from all three roles I applied for at the company. And I kindly let my connection know and she hasn’t responded to me yet.
5. The one person who no one likes because they are verbally aggressive and talk down to people got to keep their job.

Today I had a 1:1 with my boss and told her I am mentally struggling and just wanted to let her know in case I seemed off. I assured her I am going to do my work but I’m just having a hard time. She let me know I was an asset and suggested a few things. She has been supportive and even gave me some ideas of jobs I should go after. But I think it’s just everything at once. I haven’t had time to “feel my feels” and I’m feeling like I’ll never be where I want to and I don’t know how to keep positive while I am feeling this way.
You don’t have to immediately feel positive. You can wallow for a bit!

But keep in mind that layoffs are often about roles — meaning that an organization looks at what positions it can most afford to cut, rather than targeting specific people. If you have to have a Job Title X to do the organization’s work but if forced to could get by without a Job Title Y, then the person in Job Y is getting cut, even if they’re excellent at their work and even if everyone loves them. (This isn’t always the case; sometimes organizations use layoffs as opportunity to move out people who they’ve been wanting to get rid of regardless. But if you find yourself looking around and thinking, “Why on earth was it me and not Cecil?” this may be the answer.)

And the other part of the answer may be your note that this organization is a disaster! By definition, organizations that are disasters are much likely to make bad decisions about this kind of thing. So in that light, the action is perfectly in keeping with what you already knew.

As for the person who wrote you the letter of recommendation but hasn’t responded since you updated her: it’s very likely not about you at all and might be about things completely unrelated to you in her life right now. She wrote you an amazing letter, after all; you can safely assume she’s not blowing you off for the hell of it. (Also, for what it’s worth, your boyfriend and best friend shouldn’t have assured you the letter would guarantee you an interview; there’s no way to know that kind of thing from the outside.)

There are some advantages to getting advance notice of a layoff (a head start on job searching, more time to get your finances in order, etc.) but the downside very much is that it’s hard to go on working normally with people when your days are numbered, and not through your own choice. I think you’re expecting too much of yourself if you think you’re supposed to carry on exactly like you were before learned about the layoff.

It’s okay and normal that you don’t feel as engaged or focused. Most people wouldn’t! Do what you need to do to leave with your work in reasonably good shape and so you stay on good terms, but you certainly don’t need to be going above and beyond during this period.
And it’s okay that you’re not feeling positive right now! This is a blow. Take some time to absorb it without putting pressure on yourself to instantly bounce back.
